title: Shove-its, Kickflips and Heelflips
bigQuestion: How can a skater make a board spin or flip in the air and still land on it?

story.title: Wheels Down Again
story.kicker: A board spins under a jumping skater and lands wheels-down, and a friend asks how.
paragraphs: At the edge of the flat section, Ana popped and the board spun half a turn beneath her. It landed wheels-down, and she landed on it, rolling away with the old tail now in front. Her friend Marcus stopped pushing. He had seen the board turn, but Ana's body had not turned at all. How did the board come back around under her?

Ana stepped off and set the board on the grass beside the court. She showed him the back foot first. It did not just push down. It pushed down and swept backward, like scraping something off the ground behind her. The front foot barely did anything. It lifted out of the way and waited.

Then she showed him a different move, slowly, with no pop at all. Her front foot slid up the board and brushed off the edge of the nose. The board rolled over on the grass like a log, once, and came to rest grip tape up. That one, she said, is the start of a kickflip. The shove-it spins flat. The kickflip rolls.

Marcus held on to the fence and tried the flat spin on the grass. His first scoop sent the board barely a quarter turn. His second sent it all the way around and past. On the fifth try it stopped right at half a turn, nose and tail swapped. He looked up and grinned. Then he asked how long it takes to learn a kickflip.
story.think: How was the board's movement in Ana's shove-it different from its movement in her kickflip on the grass?

lessons.title: A Flat Spin Under Your Feet
lessons.mainIdea: In a pop shove-it, the board spins half a turn flat under you, around a vertical axis, while your body jumps straight up.
reading: Watch a *pop shove-it* from above. The skater pops, the board spins half a turn, and the nose and tail trade places. The skater lands on it again, now with the old tail in front. The board stays flat the whole time, grip tape up. It never flips over.

A half turn is 180 degrees, because a full circle is 360 degrees. The board turns around an *axis*, an imaginary line that something spins around. For a shove-it, the line goes straight up and down through the middle of the deck. This is the *vertical axis*. Picture a pencil stuck down through the center of the board, and the board turning around it like a spinning plate.

Your body does not spin with the board. You jump straight up and keep facing the same way, and only the board turns beneath you. So the trick needs two things: a pop to get the board off the ground, and a scoop to make it spin. A plain shove-it, with no pop, just spins the board flat along the ground.

words.d: a trick in which the skater pops the board and it spins 180 degrees flat beneath the skater
an imaginary line that an object turns around
a line running straight up and down through the middle of the deck; shove-its spin around it

look.title: How Far Shove-its Spin
look.cite: The number in each trick's name gives its spin; a full circle is 360 degrees
look.prompt: How many half turns does the board make in a 360 shove-it? In a 540 shove-it?

check.q: How far does the board spin in a pop shove-it?
check.why: A pop shove-it is a half turn, 180 degrees, so the nose and tail trade places.

check.q: Around which axis does the board spin in a shove-it?
choices: The long axis, from nose to tail
The axle of the back wheels
The short axis, across the deck
A vertical axis, straight up and down through the deck
check.why: The board stays flat and turns like a spinning plate, around a line straight up and down through its middle.

check.q: What does the skater's body do during a pop shove-it?
choices: Jumps straight up and keeps facing the same way
Spins 180 degrees along with the board
Leans far back over the tail
check.why: Only the board turns. The skater jumps straight up and lands facing the same direction.

lessons.title: The Scoop
lessons.mainIdea: For a backside pop shove-it, the back foot pops and scoops the tail behind you while the front foot lifts out of the way.
reading: Set your feet first. Put the ball of your back foot on the tail, near its toe-side edge. Your front foot rests lightly near the front bolts. The front foot does very little in this trick. It lifts away and then comes back down.

Now the motion. First crouch. Next, pop the tail down and at the same moment sweep it backward, behind you, toward your heel side. This sweeping push is the *scoop*. Your back foot moves as if it were scraping mud off the ground behind you. Then jump straight up and lift your front foot, so the board can spin freely beneath it.

This version is the *backside* pop shove-it, because the tail swings around behind your back. Most skaters learn it first. The *frontside* version scoops the tail forward, in front of your toes. Many skaters find the frontside spin harder to watch and catch. Both spin 180 degrees around the vertical axis.

The scoop gives the board a turning push. A push that makes something turn is a *torque*. The farther from the center of the turn the push lands, the more turning it gives. That is why the back foot scoops at the end of the tail, far from the middle of the deck.

words.d: the sweeping push of the back foot that makes the board spin in a shove-it
turning so the board or body swings around behind the skater's back
turning so the board or body swings around in front of the skater's toes
a turning push; torque equals force times the distance from the center of the turn

look.title: The Shove-it, Step by Step
look.text: Step 1: crouch, with the ball of the back foot near the toe-side edge of the tail. Step 2: pop and scoop the tail backward, behind you. Step 3: jump straight up and lift the front foot. Step 4: watch the board turn under you until the old tail is in front. Step 5: land with both feet over the bolts, knees bent.
look.prompt: On grass, do steps 1 and 2 with your front foot on the ground. How hard did you need to scoop to get exactly half a turn?

check.q: In a backside pop shove-it, which way does the back foot scoop the tail?
choices: Forward, in front of your toes
Backward, behind you toward your heel side
check.why: Backside means the tail swings around behind your back, so the back foot sweeps it backward.

check.q: What does the front foot do in a pop shove-it?
choices: Stays pressed down on the bolts
Lifts away so the board can spin, then comes back down
check.why: The back foot does the work. The front foot gets out of the way and lands again.

check.q: Why does the back foot scoop at the end of the tail?
choices: The tail is lighter than the rest of the board
The grip tape is rougher there
A push farther from the center gives more torque
check.why: Torque equals force times distance, so a push far from the middle gives more turning.

lessons.title: Practicing the Shove-it
lessons.mainIdea: Learn the shove-it on grass first, then rolling slowly, and fix problems one at a time.
reading: With your helmet buckled and pads on, start on grass or carpet. Practice the scoop alone, with your front foot on the ground beside the board. Scoop the tail and watch the board spin half a turn. Then step on with both feet over the bolts. This teaches the back foot how hard to scoop.

Next try the whole trick on the grass: crouch, pop and scoop, jump straight up, watch the board turn, and land on it. Then try it rolling slowly on smooth, flat ground. Keep your shoulders still and facing the same way. If your shoulders turn, your body follows the board and you land sideways.

Problem: the board spins too far, past 180 degrees. Fix: scoop more gently. Problem: the board turns only a quarter turn. Fix: scoop harder and farther behind you. Problem: the board lands behind you. Fix: you jumped backward, so jump straight up. Each try is *rotation* practice, learning how much push gives how much turn.

words.d: turning around an axis, measured in degrees
a turn of 90 degrees, one fourth of a full circle

look.title: Three Scoops on the Grass
look.text: Scoop 1 is soft, and the board turns about a quarter turn and stops sideways. Scoop 2 is hard, and the board turns all the way around and a bit past. Scoop 3 is in between, and the board stops with the nose and tail swapped, exactly half a turn. The skater's shoulders never move.
look.prompt: Try three scoops of different strengths on grass. Describe how far the board turned each time.

check.q: What is a good first step for learning the shove-it?
choices: Scoop the tail on grass with the front foot on the ground
Try it with your eyes closed
check.why: Scooping alone on grass teaches the back foot how hard to push before you jump.

check.q: The board spins past 180 degrees. What is the fix?
check.why: Too much scoop gives too much turn, so a softer scoop stops it at half a turn.

check.q: Why should you keep your shoulders still?
choices: So your body does not turn with the board and you land straight
check.why: If the shoulders turn, the body follows the board and you land sideways.

lessons.title: Kickflip Foot Position
lessons.mainIdea: For a kickflip, the back foot sits on the tail as for an ollie, and the front foot sits angled just behind the front bolts.
reading: A *kickflip* is an ollie in which the board also rolls over once in the air. Because it starts with the same pop, you need a steady ollie first. In the early 1980s Rodney Mullen worked out many tricks on flat ground, building on his flat-ground ollie, and flip tricks grew from that work. Today the kickflip is often the first flip trick skaters learn.

Back foot: the ball of the foot on the tail, as in an ollie. Some skaters move it a little toward the toe side. Front foot: just behind the front bolts, angled about 45 degrees so the toes point partly toward the nose. The foot sits near the middle of the board, not hanging off.

The angle matters because the front foot will slide up and off the nose's corner on the *toe side*, the long edge in front of your toes. A foot set straight across the board tends to make an ollie with no flip. A foot set too far back leaves no room to slide. Try a few spots on grass to find the one that feels natural.

words.d: an ollie in which the front foot flicks off the toe-side edge of the nose so the board rolls over once
the long edge of the board in front of the skater's toes
the long edge of the board behind the skater's heels

look.title: Ollie Feet and Kickflip Feet
look.text: Picture two boards side by side, seen from above. On the first, set for an ollie, the front foot lies straight across the board, a hand's width behind the front bolts. On the second, set for a kickflip, the front foot is turned about 45 degrees, toes aimed partly toward the nose. On both boards the back foot sits in the same place on the tail.
look.prompt: Stand in both stances on grass. How does turning the front foot change where it can slide?

check.q: What skill should you have before trying a kickflip?
check.why: The kickflip starts with the same pop as an ollie.

check.q: How is the front foot set for a kickflip?
choices: Angled about 45 degrees, just behind the front bolts
check.why: The angle lets the front foot slide up and off the toe-side corner of the nose.

check.q: What is the toe side of the board?
choices: The end behind the back bolts
The long edge in front of your toes
check.why: The toe side is the long edge in front of your toes; the heel side is the edge behind your heels.

lessons.title: The Flick
lessons.mainIdea: The front foot slides up and flicks off the toe-side corner of the nose, giving a torque that rolls the board around its long axis.
reading: First crouch. Next pop the tail exactly as in an ollie. Then slide your front foot up toward the nose, and near the top, *flick* it off the toe-side corner of the nose. The flick goes forward and out to the side, past the front of your toes. Then pull both knees up so the board can turn under you.

The flick pushes down on the very edge of the board. A deck is about 20 centimeters wide, so its edge is about 10 centimeters from the middle. A push there makes a torque around the board's *long axis*, the line from nose to tail. Torque = force × distance from the axis. A 20 N flick at 0.10 m gives 20 × 0.10 = 2 N·m. The same flick only 0.02 m from the middle gives 20 × 0.02 = 0.4 N·m, one fifth as much.

Why does the board roll over so easily? Most of its mass sits close to the long axis, because the deck is narrow. Mass close to an axis is easy to turn. Turning the board end over end would be much harder, because the nose and tail sit far from its middle.

A light flick is enough. Many learners kick too hard, and the board flips twice or flies away. Aim for one full roll, 360 degrees, while you are in the air. If the board keeps turning past one roll, the flick was too strong; if it stops halfway, it was too weak.

words.d: a quick brushing kick off the edge of the board that makes it flip
the line running from nose to tail through the middle of the board; kickflips and heelflips roll around it

look.title: Where the Flick Lands
look.cite: Worked example: a 20 N flick; torque = force × distance from the long axis
look.prompt: What would the torque be for the same 20 N flick at 0.06 m? Show the multiplication.

check.q: Where does the front foot flick in a kickflip?
choices: Off the heel-side edge of the tail
Off the toe-side corner of the nose
check.why: The front foot slides up and flicks off the toe-side corner of the nose.

check.q: A 20 N flick lands 0.10 m from the long axis. What is the torque?
check.why: Torque = force × distance = 20 × 0.10 = 2 N·m.

check.q: Why does the board roll easily around its long axis?
choices: Most of its mass is close to that line
check.why: The deck is narrow, so its mass sits close to the long axis, and mass near an axis is easy to turn.

lessons.title: Kickflip Problems and Fixes
lessons.mainIdea: Most kickflip problems come from flicking too hard or too soft, not jumping high enough, or leaning back.
reading: Problem: the board flips halfway and lands upside down. Fix: flick a little harder and farther out to the side, and pop higher so the board has more time. Problem: the board flips twice or shoots away. Fix: flick more softly, because the board needs only a light brush.

Problem: the board hits your *shins*. Fix: jump higher and pull your knees up sooner, and flick out to the side rather than straight forward. Some learners wear shin guards at this stage. Problem: the board lands far in front of you. Fix: you leaned back, so keep your shoulders over the board and jump straight up.

Problem: the board flips, but you are afraid to put your feet back on it. Fix: practice on grass, where the board cannot roll away. When you see the grip tape come around, step down with both feet over the bolts. If a try goes wrong, step off to the side and land on your feet, knees bent.

Flip tricks need *air time*. A 0.30 m ollie lasts about 0.49 seconds. To finish one 360 degree flip with time left to catch it, the board might turn in 0.30 s. That means 360 ÷ 0.30 = 1,200 degrees each second. A higher pop gives more time and makes the catch easier.

words.d: the fronts of the lower legs, below the knees
how long the skater and board stay off the ground during a trick

look.title: How Fast the Board Must Roll
look.cite: Worked example: one full flip of 360 degrees ÷ the time it takes
look.prompt: Which row leaves the most time to catch the board from a 0.49 second ollie? How much time is left?

check.q: The kickflip flips twice and shoots away. What is the fix?
choices: Move the back foot onto the nose
check.why: Two flips mean too much flick; the board needs only a light brush.

check.q: The board keeps hitting your shins. What helps?
choices: Jump higher and pull your knees up sooner
Flick straight down at the bolts
check.why: Lifting the knees sooner and higher gets your legs out of the board's path.

check.q: A board must turn 360 degrees in 0.30 seconds. How fast must it roll?
check.why: 360 ÷ 0.30 = 1,200 degrees per second.

lessons.title: Heelflip Foot Position
lessons.mainIdea: For a heelflip, the front foot points across the board with the toes slightly over the toe-side edge, so the heel can reach the other edge.
reading: A *heelflip* is the kickflip's partner. The board also rolls once around its long axis. This time the front heel does the flick instead of the side of the foot. Because the push lands on the opposite edge, the board rolls in the opposite direction from a kickflip.

Back foot: the ball of the foot on the tail, as in an ollie. Front foot: just behind the front bolts, pointing straight across the board. Let the toes hang slightly over the toe-side edge. In this spot, the heel sits near the heel-side edge, where it can catch the corner of the nose.

Check the stance on grass before you pop. Slide your front foot forward and swing your heel out over the heel side. If your heel cannot reach past the edge, move the foot slightly toward the toe side. The stance should feel balanced and steady, not tippy.

words.d: an ollie in which the front heel flicks off the heel-side edge of the nose so the board rolls over once
the reverse way; a heelflip rolls the reverse way from a kickflip

look.title: Kickflip Feet and Heelflip Feet
look.text: Picture the front foot from above on two boards. For the kickflip, the foot is angled about 45 degrees, ready to slide off the toe-side corner of the nose. For the heelflip, the foot points straight across the board, toes just over the toe-side edge and heel near the heel-side edge. The back foot is the same on both.
look.prompt: Set up both stances on grass. Which edge of the board is your heel closest to in the heelflip stance?

check.q: Which part of the foot flicks the board in a heelflip?
choices: The side of the front foot
check.why: In a heelflip the front heel does the flick, off the heel-side edge of the nose.

check.q: Where do the front toes go for a heelflip?
choices: Hanging slightly over the toe-side edge
check.why: With the toes just over the toe-side edge, the heel sits near the heel-side edge, ready to flick.

check.q: How does a heelflip's roll compare with a kickflip's?
choices: It spins flat like a shove-it
It rolls in the opposite direction
check.why: The heel pushes the opposite edge, so the board rolls the opposite way around the same long axis.

lessons.title: The Heel Flick
lessons.mainIdea: Pop, then kick the front heel forward and out off the heel-side corner of the nose, and let the board roll.
reading: First crouch. Next pop the tail as in an ollie. Then slide your front foot up and kick your heel forward and out, so it brushes off the heel-side corner of the nose. The kick goes away from your toes, out over the heel side. Then lift both knees so the board can roll beneath you.

Compare the two flicks. In a kickflip, the push goes down on the toe-side *edge*. In a heelflip, the push goes down on the heel-side edge. Each push makes a torque around the long axis. Because the pushes land on opposite edges, the torques turn opposite ways, and so does the board.

Problem: the board shoots forward. Fix: kick more out to the side than forward. Problem: the board turns sideways while it flips. Fix: keep your shoulders lined up with the board. Problem: the board only half flips. Fix: get your heel all the way to the edge before you kick. Every *flip trick* rewards a steady pop first.

words.d: one of the two long sides of the deck: the toe-side edge or the heel-side edge
a trick in which the board rolls or spins under the skater's feet in the air

look.title: Two Flicks, Two Directions
look.text: Hold a skateboard in front of you by its nose and tail, grip tape up. Press down on the edge nearest you and the board rolls one way. Press down on the far edge and it rolls the other way. The kickflip presses one long edge and the heelflip presses the other, so the board rolls in opposite directions.
look.prompt: Try this with a board held off the ground. Which edge did you press to copy a heelflip, the toe-side edge or the heel-side edge?

check.q: In a heelflip, which way does the heel kick?
choices: Forward and out over the heel side
Up into the air without touching the board
check.why: The heel brushes off the heel-side corner of the nose, kicking forward and out.

check.q: Why do a kickflip and a heelflip roll in opposite directions?
choices: One is done regular and the other goofy
The pushes land on opposite edges, so the torques turn opposite ways
Kickflips do not use the long axis
check.why: The kickflip pushes the toe-side edge and the heelflip pushes the heel-side edge.

check.q: The heelflip board shoots forward. What is the fix?
choices: Kick more out to the side than forward
Move the back foot onto the nose
check.why: A kick aimed too far forward pushes the board ahead, so aim it out to the side.

lessons.title: Telling Flips Apart
lessons.mainIdea: Flip tricks are named by which part of the foot flicks and which edge gets the push, and they can be mixed with shove-it spins.
reading: Skaters name flip tricks by what the front foot does. A kickflip uses the side of the front foot and the toe-side edge. A heelflip uses the heel and the heel-side edge. Both start with an ollie pop, and both roll the board 360 degrees around the long axis.

Many skaters find one of the two easier. Neither is more correct, and learning both gives you control in both directions. Watching a friend from the front shows the difference. In a kickflip, the edge nearest the toes dips first. In a heelflip, the edge nearest the heels dips first.

Flips can be mixed with spins. A *varial kickflip* adds a pop shove-it's 180 degree spin to a kickflip. A *360 flip*, also called a tre flip, adds a full 360 degree shove-it spin to a kickflip. These tricks turn the board around the long axis and the vertical axis at once. Skaters usually learn them only after the single tricks feel steady.

words.d: a kickflip combined with the 180 degree flat spin of a pop shove-it
a kickflip combined with a full 360 degree shove-it spin; also called a tre flip

look.title: Watching From the Front
look.text: Stand in front of a friend who is doing slow flicks on grass. On one try, the edge nearest their toes dips and the board rolls toward you. On the next, their heel kicks out behind them, the far edge dips, and the board rolls the other way. Same board, same long axis, opposite rolls.
look.prompt: Watch two slow flicks on grass. Name each one as a kickflip or a heelflip, and say which clue told you.

check.q: Which edge gets the push in a kickflip?
check.why: The side of the front foot flicks down on the toe-side edge.

check.q: What is a varial kickflip?
choices: A kickflip combined with a pop shove-it's 180 degree spin
A kickflip done on a rail
check.why: A varial kickflip mixes a kickflip's roll with a pop shove-it's half-turn spin.

check.q: A 360 flip combines a kickflip with what?
check.why: The 360 flip, or tre flip, adds a full 360 degree shove-it spin to a kickflip.

lessons.title: The Three Axes of a Board
lessons.mainIdea: Every board trick turns around one or more of three axes: the long axis, the short axis and the vertical axis.
reading: Picture three sticks pushed through the center of a skateboard. One runs from nose to tail: the long axis. One runs across the deck from the toe-side edge to the heel-side edge: the *short axis*. One runs straight up and down through the deck: the vertical axis. Every turn a board makes in the air happens around one of these lines, or more than one at once.

Each trick family uses a different axis. Kickflips and heelflips roll the board around the long axis. Shove-its spin it around the vertical axis. The ollie's nose-up tilt is a small turn around the short axis. A *combination trick* such as the 360 flip uses two axes at the same time.

The axes also explain how hard a turn is. A board is about 80 centimeters long and about 20 centimeters wide. Around the long axis, all of its mass sits within about 10 centimeters, so it rolls easily. Around the short and vertical axes, the nose and tail are about 40 centimeters away, so the board resists turning more. Scientists call this resistance *rotational inertia*.

words.d: the line running across the deck from the toe-side edge to the heel-side edge
a trick that mixes two moves, such as a flip and a spin, at the same time
how strongly an object resists being turned; it is larger when mass sits far from the axis

look.title: Three Pencils Through a Board
look.text: Imagine a small model board with three pencils stuck through its center. The first pencil points from nose to tail. The second points across, from edge to edge. The third points straight up. Twirl the model around each pencil in turn. Around the first, it rolls like a log. Around the second, it turns end over end. Around the third, it spins flat like a plate.
look.prompt: Name the pencil, or axis, for each of these: kickflip, pop shove-it, heelflip.

check.q: A heelflip rolls the board around which axis?
check.why: Kickflips and heelflips both roll the board around the long axis, from nose to tail.

check.q: A pop shove-it spins the board around which axis?
check.why: A shove-it spins flat, around a line straight up and down through the deck.

check.q: Why is the board harder to spin around the vertical axis than to roll around the long axis?
choices: Its nose and tail are far from that axis, so its rotational inertia is larger
It is lighter when it spins flat
Gravity pulls only on the nose
check.why: Mass far from an axis resists turning more, and the nose and tail are about 40 cm from the vertical axis.

lessons.title: Catching the Board
lessons.mainIdea: Catching means stopping the board's turn with your feet as the grip tape comes back up, then landing over the bolts.
reading: A flip trick is finished only when you catch it. To *catch* means to stop the board's turning with your feet and land on it. Watch the board the whole time it is in the air. When the grip tape comes back up under you, that is the moment to put your feet down.

In a kickflip, many skaters catch with the back foot first. The back foot comes down on the tail and stops the roll. The front foot then lands over the front bolts. In a pop shove-it, both feet usually come down together once the board has turned 180 degrees. Either way, aim for both feet over the bolts with your knees bent.

Stopping a turn takes a torque in the opposite direction, and your feet supply it. When your shoe presses on the turning board, the push of your foot and the grip of the tape slow the turn. A firm, flat foot stops the turn cleanly. A foot that lands on the *edge* of a still-turning board can tip it and roll your ankle.

After the catch, bend your knees, stay low and roll away. Rolling away steady is part of landing the trick. Keep your shoulders over the board while you roll, because leaning back sends it out in front of you. If the board wobbles, look ahead and let your bent knees soak up the bumps.

words.d: to stop a turning board with your feet and land on it
one of the long sides of the deck, where a foot can tip the board if it lands there

look.title: Watching for the Grip Tape
look.text: A kickflip from the skater's eyes: the board leaves the ground and turns over, showing the dark wheels and trucks for a blink. Then a strip of black grip tape swings back into view. That is the cue. The back foot drops onto the tail, the roll stops, and the front foot comes down over the front bolts.
look.prompt: On grass, flick the board without jumping and say 'now' when you see the grip tape come back up. How quickly does it happen?

check.q: What does it mean to catch a flip trick?
choices: To grab the board with your hands
To stop the board's turning with your feet and land on it
To pick up the board after a fall
check.why: Catching uses the feet to stop the board's turn so you can land on it.

check.q: When should you put your feet down on a flipping board?
choices: When the wheels face the sky
When the grip tape comes back up under you
Only after the board hits the ground
check.why: The grip tape coming back up shows the board has finished its turn and is ready to stand on.

check.q: Why should your foot land flat over the bolts, not on an edge?
choices: It makes the board flip again
A foot on an edge can tip the board and roll your ankle
check.why: A firm, flat foot over the bolts stops the turn cleanly; landing on an edge can tip the board.

lessons.title: Practicing Flips Slowly
lessons.mainIdea: Practice flip motions slowly and in parts, on grass and holding a support, before trying them rolling.
reading: Practice the flick standing still on grass or carpet, with your helmet buckled and wrist guards on. Hold a friend's shoulder or a sturdy fence. Without popping, slide your front foot up and flick off the nose. Watch how the board rolls. Keep going until the flick sends the board around once, not twice and not halfway.

Next add a small pop while still holding on. Then let go and try the whole trick on the grass. Try it rolling slowly on smooth, flat ground only after you can catch it on grass several times in a row. Each step gets you ready for the next.

Slow practice helps because your brain learns a movement as a pattern. Repeating the right pattern many times makes it *automatic*, so it happens without thinking during the fast real trick. People often call this *muscle memory*, though the learning really happens in the brain. Rushing to full speed too soon can build a habit of the wrong motion.
Rest matters too. Flip practice is hard on ankles and shins. Stop when you feel tired, because tired legs pop lower and land less steadily. Ending on a good try helps you remember how it felt.

words.d: done without having to think about each step
the everyday name for a movement that has become automatic through practice; the learning happens in the brain

look.title: Four Sessions Toward a Kickflip
look.text: Session 1: flicks on grass without popping, holding a fence, until the board rolls once. Session 2: small pops with the flick, still holding on. Session 3: the whole kickflip on grass without holding on, catching with the back foot first. Session 4: if catches on grass come several times in a row, slow rolling tries on smooth, flat ground.
look.prompt: Which session sounds hardest to you? What could you add between two sessions to make the jump smaller?

check.q: What should you practice first for a kickflip?
choices: The flick, standing still on grass while holding a support
check.why: The flick alone, on grass and holding on, is the smallest first step.

check.q: When is it time to try a flip trick while rolling?
choices: After your first try on grass
After you can catch it on grass several times in a row
Before you try it on grass
check.why: Steady catches on grass show the pattern is ready for a moving board.

check.q: Why does slow, repeated practice help?
choices: It wears in the grip tape
check.why: Repeating the right pattern makes it automatic, so it happens during the fast real trick.

review.q: How do a pop shove-it and a kickflip differ?
choices: The shove-it spins flat around the vertical axis; the kickflip rolls around the long axis
The kickflip spins flat; the shove-it rolls over
review.why: The shove-it turns like a spinning plate; the kickflip rolls over like a log.

review.q: In a backside pop shove-it, what does the back foot do?
choices: Pops and scoops the tail behind you
review.why: The back foot pops the tail and sweeps it backward, behind your back.

review.q: In a kickflip, the front foot flicks off which part of the board?
choices: The heel-side edge of the tail
The toe-side corner of the nose
review.why: The side of the front foot slides up and flicks off the toe-side corner of the nose.

review.q: What does the heel do in a heelflip?
choices: Kicks off the heel-side corner of the nose
review.why: The front heel brushes forward and out off the heel-side corner of the nose.

review.q: A 25 N flick lands 0.08 m from the long axis. What is the torque?
Which axis does the ollie's nose-up tilt turn around?
choices: The wheel axle of the front truck
review.why: The nose rising and tail dropping is a turn around the short axis, across the deck.

review.q: What is the cue to catch a kickflip?
choices: The grip tape coming back up under you
review.why: When the grip tape comes back up, the board has finished its roll and is ready to land on.

review.q: Why does a higher pop make flip tricks easier?
choices: It gives more air time to finish the flip and catch it
It stops the board from turning
review.why: A higher ollie stays in the air longer, so the board has time to turn and you have time to catch it.
